paras: The lynching of Jim Harris was the killing of a Black man at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of April 30, 1888, by men a Mississippi weekly described only as "citizens." Harris had been accused of criminally assaulting a white woman, Mrs. M. Simmons, the night before, and he refused to confess before he was killed. A New Orleans Picayune dispatch carried the case to papers from Georgia to Dakota, while Mississippi papers added that he was hanged at the courthouse door and that officials were criticized for trying to save a white accomplice.

Harris, described as "colored," was accused of a criminal assault on Mrs. M. Simmons in Vicksburg on Sunday night, April 29. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star alone described the attacker as "a negro burglar" and the crime as "a brutal outrage upon a white woman." According to the dispatch, Harris was said to have had two accomplices, but he would name neither of them.

A special dispatch from Vicksburg to the New Orleans Picayune reported that Harris was lynched on the night of Monday, April 30, and that he "refused to confess to the last." The Southern Herald, a Mississippi weekly, wrote that he was "lynched by citizens," and the Grenada Sentinel placed the lynching "in front of the court house door." The Greenville Times said that he was "hung," the only text to name the method. None of these reports gave the number of men involved or named any of them.

On May 5 the Greenville Times wrote that "efforts by the officials to save his white accomplice have been severely criticised," the only mention in the coverage of a white accomplice or of any official action. The paper named neither the accomplice nor the officials, and no report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage.

The Picayune special first appeared outside Louisiana on May 1, in the Washington Evening Star under the headline "Lynched for Criminal Assault" and in the Alexandria Gazette, which printed it beside the lynching of Henry Pope at Summerville, Georgia. The Savannah Morning News headed it "Lynching a Ravisher" on May 2, and the Barton County Democrat in Kansas later grouped it with the Pope case under "Negro Lynchings" and "Another Case." Condensed versions ran in news-summary columns, where the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer placed Vicksburg in "Va." and the Daily Republican and the Westminster Democratic Advocate placed it in "Tennessee." A one-line ready-print brief saying Harris was lynched "on the 1st" ran in the Kenosha Telegraph on May 4 and in Minnesota and Dakota weeklies as late as May 26.

Every version stated the accusation as fact, saying that Harris "criminally assaulted" Mrs. Simmons rather than that he was accused of doing so. Mississippi papers approved of the killing: the Greenville Times wrote that there was "no sort of doubt about the right man being hung" and that the offense admitted "no plea in defense or mitigation." The Pascagoula Democrat-Star said the accused had been "expeditiously lynched," and the Grenada Sentinel remarked that "Judge Lynch" had "paid his respects" in Vicksburg and Claiborne County that week "on two negroes for committing rape."

Most reports named the victim Jim or James Harris, but the Southern Herald called him "Tom Harris"; the Picayune dispatch, the earliest and fullest account, used Jim. The dispatch and the Southern Herald put the lynching on Monday night, while the ready-print brief gave "the 1st," the date of the dispatch. The accusation was a criminal assault in the wire reports but a burglary and "brutal outrage" in the Pascagoula paper.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Harris
bases: Every report says Harris, accused of assaulting a white woman, was 'lynched', a Mississippi weekly says 'by citizens', and the Greenville Times says he was hung (A1, A9, A11, A16).

Harris was killed without trial in reprisal for an alleged criminal assault, 'lynched by citizens' and hanged in front of the court house door (A1, A9, A10, A11); no report gives the number of men, but the plural 'citizens' and the public site point to a group.

The wire reports all derive from one Picayune special (A1, A3, A5), but Mississippi weeklies with their own wording and details (A9, A10, A11, A16) agree that a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman was lynched at Vicksburg that Monday night.

accounts.gist: Jim Harris, colored, who criminally assaulted Mrs. M. Simmons Sunday night, was lynched last night; he refused to confess and would say nothing of two reported accomplices.

accounts.label: Mississippi weeklies
accounts.gist: He was lynched 'by citizens' Monday night in front of the court house door; one calls him a burglar who outraged a white woman, and one says officials were criticized for trying to save his white accomplice.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Picayune special or one-line summaries stating as fact that Harris 'criminally assaulted' Mrs. Simmons, under headlines such as 'Lynching a Ravisher'.

The Greenville Times said there was 'no sort of doubt about the right man being hung' and the offense admitted 'no plea in defense or mitigation'; the Pascagoula Democrat-Star said he was 'expeditiously lynched'.

conflicts.note: The Picayune special, the earliest and fullest report, names him Jim Harris.
The ready-print brief appears to use the May 1 dispatch date; the dispatch and a Mississippi weekly both say Monday night.
The Tennessee and Virginia readings are errors in condensed summaries; the datelines and Mississippi papers place Vicksburg in Mississippi.
